utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If the Chamber could go into private session before we begin.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Before proceeding with the trial, the Chamber would like to read out an oral order on, oral decision, on the Prosecution's 92 bis motion of the 25th of January 2006. And the order goes as follows: The Prosecution requested admission of the statements of witnesses MM-028, Ivan Jelic, and MM-068, Aleksandra Szekely, MM-072, Milan Smoljan, and MM-073, Bozica Lisak. The Defence in its response did not object to the admission of the statements. However, the Defence did object to admission of two proposed exhibits accompanying the statement of witness MM-028. In its decision on the 16th of January 2006, the Trial Chamber set out the applicable law on the admission of 92 bis statements. This law remains applicable in today's decision. The Trial Chamber finds that the statements of witnesses MM-68, MM-072, MM-073, meet the requirements as set out in Rule 92 bis of the Rules and the relevant jurisprudence. The statements are therefore admitted. The Trial Chamber further finds that the statement of witness MM-028 also meets the requirements of Rule 92 bis. However, the Defence has raised objections on the authenticity of the material associated with that statement. The Trial Chamber requests the Prosecution to obtain a further statement from the witness addressing the following questions. 1: Does the witness verify that the list depicted in the upper part of the newspaper page is in fact the list he received, signed, and handed to the mayor of Zadar. 2: Does the witness verify that the video footage regarding the attacks on the villages of Skabrnja and Nadin in November 1991, including his narrative account of those attacks and the footage of the victims arrival at a hospital in Zadar and the subsequent identification of those victims by family members have not been manipulated and are a true depiction of the events as he remembers them. The Trial Chamber will defer its decision on the motion for admission of the statement of Witness MM-4028 until such time that it has received the supplementary statement and the requested translation. Finally, the Trial Chamber requests that the Registrar assign Exhibit numbers to the statements and associated material of the statements of witnesses MM-068, MM-072, MM-073. Thank you. That's the order. Is it you, Mr. Whiting? Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It is me, Your Honour, thank you, and, of course, the Prosecution will comply with the order as soon as we can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Before we call our next witness I want to raise a small procedural matter, if I may. The Bench may have noticed in addition to what might be considered our table here, and I'd like to introduce to the Bench Mr. Peter Michael Mueller who is seated at the end of the bench. Mr. Mueller is not in fact a member of the Prosecution team. He is the lawyer for the witness, Mr. Milan Babic. He represented Mr. Babic throughout Mr. Babic's own case and also has represented him during his testimony in two previous cases here at the Tribunal. In those two previous cases he was permitted by the Bench to sit in the courtroom during the testimony, simply for purposes in case there is some reason for the witness to consult with him. I don't expect him to participate in proceedings. However, if the witness has some need during his testimony to consult and there are matters which may arise -- I don't expect it, but there are matters that may arise that might require consultation and I think it would therefore justify us having Mr. Mueller be seated here in the courtroom during the testimony of Mr. Babic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Whiting. Thank you very much, Mr. Mueller. You're welcome to sit there next to your client. Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: With that resolved, the Prosecution calls Mr. Milan Babic as the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. May Mr. Babic come to the stand, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May Mr. Babic please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Whiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic you may be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Babic, can you understand me clearly in your own language?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon. I do understand you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, if at any time you're unable to understand me in your own language or if you're unable to understand my question, please tell me.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you please state your name?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: I'm Milan Babic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm going to go through your background quickly if I may. Could you confirm that you were born in 1956 in Kukar in the municipality of Sinj in Croatia, you are married, you have two children --

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: -- you're a dentist by profession, and by the end of 1989 you were one of the acting directors of a primary health centre in Knin; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, I want to start by going through the various positions you held after 1990. But before the war, were you a member of the League of Communists of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In February of 1990, did you attend the founding rally of the Serbian Democratic Party or the SDS in Knin?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you assume any positions within the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you tell us what they were?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: I became a member of the main board of the SDS, and I became the president of the municipal board of the SDS in Knin in that spring.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When did you become a member of the main board?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: At the founding assembly in February 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You said that you became president of the municipal board in Knin in that spring. Spring of which year, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you assume any other positions thereafter within the SDS, in 1990 or 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: In March 1991, I became a member of the regional board of the SDS for Krajina. And in November 1992, I became president of the SDS for Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How long did you hold that position?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: I was president of the SDS in Krajina between November 1992 and August 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Aside from your positions in the SDS, did you assume any positions in the Knin municipality?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you tell us what they were, please?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: In May 1990 I was elected president of the municipality of -- of the municipal assembly of Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How long did you hold that position?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Until April 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In 1990 did you have a position in the association of municipalities of Northern Dalmatia and Lika?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was the president of the temporary presidency of the community of the municipality of Northern Dalmatia and Lika.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In July of 1990, it's been agreed that the Serbian National Council was established. Did you have a position in the Serbian National Council?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: I was the president of the Serbian National Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When did you become the president?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: On the 31st of July 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic it's also been agreed that on the 21st of December 1990 the Serbian Autonomous District of Krajina otherwise known as the SAO Krajina was established. Did you hold a position in the SAO Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was president of the temporary executive council of SAO Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And from what date to what date?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Between the 21st of December 1990 and the 30th of April 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you hold any position after that -- after the 30th of April 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: I was elected president of the executive council of the SAO Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And from what date to what date did you hold that position?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: From the 30th of April 1991 until the 29th of May 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you assume another position on the 29th of May 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes. I became the president -- the head of the government of the SAO Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How long did you hold that position?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Until the 19th of December 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It's been agreed that on the 19th of December 1991, the Republic of Serbian Krajina or RSK was formed. Did you hold a position in that entity?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: I was the president of the republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How long did you hold that position?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Between the 19th of December 1991 and the 16th of February 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: At the end of 1993 and the beginning of 1994, did you run for president of the RSK?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What was the result of that election?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: I won the elections in the first round but the elections were repeated and in the second round Mr. Martic won the elections and he became president of the Republic of Srpska Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In 1994 did you get a position in the government of the RSK?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: In April I became a member of the government of the Republic of Srpska Krajina and my position was the Minister of Foreign Affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Until when did you hold that position?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Until the 27th of July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you assume another position on that date?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes. I became the head of government of the Republic of Srpska Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How long did you hold that position?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: About a week, until the 4th of August 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What happened on the 4th of August 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Croatia carried out the military aggression on the Republic of Srpska Krajina and the territory of Krajina was occupied.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, I want to talk now about your own case at the Tribunal. Could you tell us how you first had contact with the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: In autumn 2001, I heard through the media that my name was mentioned in an indictment -- in the indictment against Slobodan Milosevic, in fact, as being an accessory in the joint criminal enterprise. Having heard that news, I tried to get in touch with the office of the International Tribunal in Belgrade and that's how I got in touch with the Tribunal. And later on that year, I started having contacts with the International Tribunal for the Former Yugoslavia in order to tell the truth about the events that I knew about.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: During those interviews, were you represented by counsel?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Is it the same counsel that represents you today?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Were you treated as a suspect in the interviews with the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes, and I was reminded of the fact before the start of each interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Were the interviews recorded?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: They were.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you believe that you yourself could be charged?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was a possibility of that. I assumed that I would be charged.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: During the interviews were you told anything about that by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: I was told that there was a possibility of an indictment against me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Why did you submit to those interviews?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: In order to establish the truth about the events that took place at that time and in order to fully present my own role in those events.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Were you hoping to help yourself?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: In a way, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In what way?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: I supposed that the Prosecution would get a full picture of my participation and in case I ended up as an indictee that it would represent an extenuating circumstance.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you provide documents to the Prosecution during this period of -- during these interviews?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately how many documents you provided?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: About 180.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Were these documents from the time period, that is from 1990 to 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you testify in the Milosevic case in 2002?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you recall for how many days you testified?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Approximately 12 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: On the 17th of November 2003, was an indictment confirmed against you at the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, with the assistance of the usher I would like to show the witness the indictment and perhaps it could be placed on the ELMO. This is a copy of the indictment in all three languages, in English, French, and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, do you recognise that indictment?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Is that the indictment that was confirmed against you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Don't we have the indictment on the ELMO, as you suggested?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. What's being shown on the ELMO obviously --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: -- is the B/C/S version. I'm not going to go through this indictment but I would ask that it be admitted into evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The indictment is admitted into evidence as an exhibit, and may it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number 173, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number of the B/C/S indictment. Can we give an exhibit number to the English version of that indictment, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think actually one number -- if I'm not mistaken -- I'll be corrected if I'm wrong, but I think one number can be given to all different -- all languages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If that is so, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, that can be removed from the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, on the 22nd of January 2004, did you -- we may be using the ELMO again so if we could leave it -- did you plead guilty to count 1 of the indictment, the crime of persecutions, under Article 5(H) of the Statute of the Tribunal and did you admit to having been a co-perpetrator of a joint criminal enterprise from the 1st of August 1991 until the 15th of February 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I'm not sure about the date because I think the session was on the 22nd of January and the -- afterwards, I pleaded guilty.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter apologises, we haven't heard the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. But at approximately that time, in January of 19 -- January of 2004, you agree you plead guilty; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes, concerning the first count of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Was the goal of the joint criminal enterprise to which you pled guilty the forcible removal of the majority of Croat and other non-Serb populations from approximately one-third of Croatia in order to transform that territory into a Serb-dominated state through the commission of crimes within the jurisdiction of the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: With the assistance of the usher, I would like to put a document in front of the witness. For this document, I have copies for the Chamber and the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, is this the plea agreement you entered into in your case?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you turn, please, to page 6? Is that your signature on page 6? No. I'm sorry, that -- it's page 6 of the English, please. Okay. That's actually page 7 but that's fine. Is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Was there a factual basis attached to this plea agreement, at tab 1? It's on the next page.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you agree to that factual statement?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I want to look at paragraphs -- at paragraph 8 of the plea agreement which appears on page 4 of the agreement. In English. No, not the factual statement. It's before that. It's before that. On page 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Paragraph 8, please, there at the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, it says in paragraph 8 that "Milan Babic agrees to accept responsibility for his actions and to cooperate with and to provide truthful and complete information to the Office of the Prosecutor whenever requested." At the end of that paragraph, it says "Mr. Babic agrees to testify truthfully at any trials, hearings or other proceedings before the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia, ICTY, as requested by the OTP." Did you agree to that provision?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Paragraph 10, it states, "It is understood and agreed by Milan Babic and the Prosecution that all information and testimony provided by Mr. Babic must be absolutely truthful. This means that Milan Babic must neither minimise his own actions nor fabricate someone else's involvement." Did you agree to that provision?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And in this agreement, did the Prosecution agree to recommend a sentence of no more than or, let's say, less than 11 years in your case?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, could this document be admitted into evidence, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Which document, Mr. Whiting? Is it the agreement or -- together with the factual basis for the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The whole thing, the whole thing, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document then is admitted into evidence. And may it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number 174, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, at the time you pled guilty did you make a statement before the Court?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And with the assistance of the usher could I provide Mr. Babic a document, and I have copies for the Chamber and the parties. For the record this is a portion of the transcript from the 27th of January 2004. I'm sorry, it's a portion of the transcript from January 27th, 2004, in Mr. Babic's case, which was case number IT-03-72-I, and the pages of the transcript are pages 57 and 58.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, is this the statement that you made?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you read the statement for us, please? And this has been provided to the interpreters. It is -- it was provided in addition to the -- yes. I think it's been found. So it would be of assistance to the interpreters. Let me just -- if we could just wait a moment. I see that it's moving from booth to booth here. It starts -- for the benefit of the booth it starts at "the accused." Mr. Babic, could you read the statement, please?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: I said the following. "Thank you, Your Honour. I come before this Tribunal with a deep sense of shame and remorse. I have allowed myself to take part in the worst kind of persecution of people simply because they were Croats and not Serbs. Innocent people were persecuted. Innocent people were evicted forcibly from their houses and innocent people were killed. Even I learned what had happened -- even after I had learned what had happened I kept silent. Even worse I continued in my office and I became personally responsible for the inhumane treatment of innocent people. "The regret that I feel is the pain that I have to live with for the rest of my life. These crimes and my participation therein can never be justified. I'm speechless when I have to express the depth of my remorse for what I have done, and for the effect of my sins and the effect they have had on the others. I can only hope that by expressing the truth, by admitting to my guilt and expressing the remorse, can serve as an example to those who still mistakenly believe that such inhumane acts can ever be justified. "Only truth can give the opportunity to the Serbian people to relieve themselves of its -- their collective burden of guilt. Only this an admission of guilt on their part makes it possible for me to take responsibility for all the wrongdoings that I have done. I hope that the remorse that I have expressed will make it easier for the others to bear their pain and suffering. I have come to understand that enmity and division can never make it easier nor to us live together. I have come to understand that the fact that we all belong to the same human race and that it is more important than any difference and I have come to understand that only through friendship and confidence can we live together in peace and friendship and thus make it possible for our children to live in a better world. "I've asked help from God to make it easier for me to repent and I'm thankful to God for making it possible for me to express my repentance. I ask my brothers, Croats, to forgive us, their brother Serbs, and I pray for the Serb people to turn to the future and to achieve the kind of compassion that will make it possible to forgive the crimes. And lastly, I place myself at the full disposal of this Tribunal and the international justice. Thank you very much." Those were my words then, and I stand by them even today.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Babic. You anticipated my question. On the 29th of June of 2004, were you sentenced to a period of 13 years?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before he answers that question, are we to do anything with this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think it's necessary to make it an exhibit since it's been read into the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: On the 29th of June 2004, were you sentenced by the Trial Chamber to a period of 13 years' imprisonment?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: With the assistance of the usher could I put a document in front of the witness, please? Mr. Babic, do you recognise that document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What is it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: It is the judgement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In your case?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour I would ask that be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number 175, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It can be removed from the ELMO. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, you were sentenced in that judgement to 13 years. Did you appeal that sentence?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: I did. I appealed against the amount of the sentence, the length.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you appeal the judgement itself or just the sentence?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: No, not the judgement itself but the duration of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: On the 18th of July 2005 was the sentence affirmed, the sentence of 13 years affirmed by the Appeals Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, please do not say where you are doing this but are you presently serving your sentence?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In June of 2004, did you testify in the trial of the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, those are all the questions about your case. I'm going to move on to a different subject. With the assistance of the usher, could I please show Mr. Babic the -- his 89(F) statement and I'll take care of moving that into evidence now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are we to hear anything about Momcilo Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No, just that he testified in that trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, could you look at that, please, and in particular could you look at the first document in that binder? Do you recognise that document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you sign it and initial all the pages?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What is it? What is that document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: It is a statement given by me according to the rules of the Tribunal pertaining to the knowledge I have concerning the events described in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Is the information contained in that statement true and accurate, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Is what is written in the document what you would testify to if you testified orally about those subjects?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would move that the exhibit -- into evidence, and just to be clear with respect to the Court's order on this issue, what we've done we've, of course, complied with the Court's order but this how we did it. We kept the statement as it was with all the references to all the documents, but we removed from the attachments the exhibits that the Court found should be removed, and the reason we did that is that we were afraid if we deleted them from the statement and re-numbered the statement it would start to get confusing about what the record would get confusing about what had been removed and what remained so in order to make -- to keep a clear record we kept the statement as it was and removed the exhibits, and that is what is in the binder. And I would ask that it be moved into evidence now, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The entire binder?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, the binder is the statement with the exhibits that were admitted by the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we have an objection to make. We haven't received a signed statement. According to my esteemed colleague from the OTP there were some changes and amendments made to that statement. We don't know what their contents are and it would be good if the Defence would be given a copy to see if we have any objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry, there must have been a misunderstanding, there have been no changes at all or amendments to the statement. The statement is identical to the statement that was filed with the Chamber and ruled on by the Chamber. I do understand that Defence counsel would like to have the signed version and I don't have one at hand to give him but at the break I can -- I do. I do have one, with the assistance of the usher. But I can represent to counsel and to the Bench that it is identical to the one that was filed with the Court and provided to Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, did you hear that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did, Your Honour. I will be able to confirm that only after having read the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you suggesting that your objection still stands?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. We are lagging behind so to speak because had we be given the documents before that, by this time we would have been able to state our position. But as things are now, we can't state our position as regards the statement. We can only take the word of the OTP. But we can express our position only after having read the statement, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would have thought my word would be sufficient but I have no problem deferring on this matter until a later time in the testimony. It's not a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I just wanted to get it quite clear from Mr. Milovancevic that -- are you saying that you do not accept your colleague's word on this issue, that this statement is identical to the statement that you had been given, and there has been no change to the statement? The only change is to the annexes to the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if the basis to accept written evidence is the word of the opposing party, then we have no need for the Rules of Procedure. As foreseen by the Rules, the opposing party needs to forward every piece of document they have. And I wouldn't want to find myself in a situation of being told something by the OTP that is not so. If the Chamber wishes to know the position of the Defence, and if the Defence wants to do their work seriously, then all of the material needs to be forwarded to the Defence to state their position, and therefore at this moment I cannot state our position. It is not a matter of whether I believe my colleague or not. It was an omission on their part and not on our part and now it is being represented here as our wrongdoing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Nobody is representing it as your wrongdoing. I was just asking you a question. If you will not take your colleague's word, very well, then, the ruling on this -- on the admission of the document will be made once you have confirmed with your colleague on the opposite side, Mr. Whiting. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, the first topic I want to discuss is I want to look at a map, and could that be taken from -- that can be removed from in front of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Usher, it is suggested that you can remove that whole binder from the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, I want to show a map to you and ask you some questions about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Again, I'll ask the assistance of the usher to provide two documents. For the record, the first document, a map, is 01131342. It will be familiar to the Chamber. It's identical to Exhibit 3 that is in evidence. And the reason I'm providing it in this form is that it's a much better copy and much more readable than the version that I provided before. The second document, which is 01132355 to 01132358 in the B/C/S and an attached translation, that will become clear in a moment, what that is, through the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, do you recognise this map?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you provide this map to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The document with text that is -- that accompanies the map that I've given to you and I've read out the ERN, what is that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: It was printed on -- at the -- on the back of the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So just to be clear, the original map had the map on the front and this text on the back? Is that what you're testifying to?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know who made this map and when it was made?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: It was published by the publishing company called Vojska from Belgrade. I received it after 1993, and it was supposed to reflect the situation in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you tell us anything about the publishing company Vojska?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: It was a state-owned enterprise.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know who -- are you able to tell or do you know who asked for the map to be made? Or who created the map? You've told us who published it but who created it? If you know.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I presume the Main Staff of the military of the RSK.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Why do you presume that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: I believe I saw their -- I saw somewhere that they authored this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I just clear a little point in my mind? Is it the evidence that all the documents -- all the pages from page 1 and looking now at the English version to page 13, all that information was written on the back of this map?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, the English version is slightly misleading because the English version that's been provided has -- contains the translation of both the front and the back and so it's much longer than would appear. The pages that what appeared on the back of the map are the four pages in B/C/S. So it's four pages that appeared in text on the back of the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But is the English not a translation of the four pages in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It's the English is a translation of the four pages plus all the text on the front of the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So the record is not showing it correctly when it says what is written on this document is what was written on the back of the map. The record should read, the first four pages of the English version are a translation of the B/C/S that appeared on the back of the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour that's not exactly right but I'll try to make it clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And I apologise for the confusion. And the witness should listen to this to -- so that he could confirm that it's accurate but this is my understanding of his testimony and of the exhibit. The four pages of B/C/S which are 01132355 to 2358 are the text that appeared on the back of the map. The attached English translation is longer and the first part of the English translation 01132359 to 2361, the first two and some pages are the translation of the front of the map. And that actually has already been provided to the Chamber. Starting on 01132361, it even says in there, it says "back of the map" and that is the translation of the text that appeared on the back of the map. I hope that's clear and if the witness could -- if the witness followed that and if the witness could confirm that that is in fact at least with respect to the first four pages of B/C/S, that that's in fact what was on the back of the map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. In Serbo-Croatian, I can -- I understand that it was on the back of the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And then pages 01132362 through to 01132371 are what? Constitute what?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's the translation of the four pages in B/C/S appeared on the back of the map and that are attached here, that are these first four pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Whiting, I thought you were saying that from page 0113261 below the line where it says, "Back of the map" that is where the translation concerning the back of the map commences in sequence; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's correct, Your Honour. I apologise. I misheard Your Honour, Judge mow low toe but that's correct, it starts from 2361, that's correct, to the end, to 2371, that's the translation of the four pages that appeared on the back of the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, I want to ask you some questions about the front of the map, if you would turn your attention to the front of the map, please. On the front of the map, on the lower half in the middle, there is a map that is in a blue colour of Croatia. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And is that -- and there is a legend there and do the shadings there, the blue shadings reflect the census data for 1981?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Looking at the data that is reflected on this map for 1981, was this -- was the sense -- the ethnic distribution in Croatia approximately the same in 1991 as it was in 1981?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes, roughly speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to talk to you about various regions. We've heard in this trial about various regions within Croatia. Northern Dalmatia, Lika, Kordun and Banija. We've heard some testimony about that and I want to discuss with you and ask your assistance in orienting [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It's on but it's not work,.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's not lit here, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I've been cut off!

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you need assistance before we can proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm told someone is coming to attend to the problem. There, you're on now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour let me see where I was. Okay. I was saying that we've heard about various regions within Croatia, Northern Dalmatia, Lika, Kordun and Banija, and I'd like to ask your assistance please in orienting us and the Chamber about where these regions were. And it may be helpful for the Chamber in following this testimony to have at its disposal map 3 from the map book because we are going to be talking about municipalities and I'm happy to lone my map book if -- or we have other copies to loan if anybody has forgotten their -- I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We are very grateful to the Prosecution for loaning us. It's actually not forgetfulness, it's just that we've got limited space here and we are trying to reduce our load each time we come to court.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour. I think we've provided two. Is that sufficient or is three necessary?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. As I said, map 3, it might be helpful in following this part of the testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, could you tell us which municipalities were within the region that's been -- that's referred to as Northern Dalmatia?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I just confirm, on this map; we are looking at this map?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: My questions were about that map. We've left that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, did you hear my question? Which municipalities were in the region known as Northern Dalmatia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: The municipalities of Knin, Benkovac, Obrovac, and Drnis. And something which used to be fictionally called the municipality of Zadar since 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you explain to the Chamber what you mean about -- what you're talking about when you refer to the municipality of Zadar?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly when. By the end of 1992 and in 1993, the so-called municipality of Zadar was set up. It did not have any territory as such. It was just presented to the public as being in existence because in 1991, certain Serb villages from the municipality of Zadar joined the municipality of Benkovac so they were within the framework of the municipality of Benkovac and I don't suppose they got out of that municipality and crossed over to the Zadar municipality in 1993. That's why I'm saying that it was a fictional municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When you're talking about this fictional municipality of Zadar, is it just to distinguish it -- is it the Serbian Municipality of Zadar or are you talking about the whole municipality of Zadar?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: The Serb Municipality of Zadar.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. And did that Serb Municipality of Zadar, did it occupy -- was it -- did it occupy the entire municipality of Zadar or just a part of the municipality of Zadar?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: It was supposed to be the Serb part of the municipality of Zadar.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And the villages of Skabrnja and Nadin, do you -- what area did they belong to, do you know?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Before the conflict, I'm not very sure. But I think they were either within the municipality of Zadar or Biograd [phoen], and after the armed conflict, that is to say in the autumn of 1991, they had been militarily occupied and so they became part of the territory of the SAO Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, the area that you've identified as Northern Dalmatia, do you know approximately what the ethnic composition of this area was in 1990 and 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: According to my assessment, 80 per cent Serbs and 20 per cent Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The next area I want to ask you about is the area of Lika. Which municipalities made up the area of Lika?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: The region of Lika was made up of Donji Lapac, Gracac, Titova Korenica, and Plaski. Those were the municipalities there. Also, the municipality of Vrhovine which was set up at a certain point. Or rather at one point Vrhovine and Plaski belonged to the municipality of Titova Korenica, and then afterwards they separated and they were set up as separate municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. So these municipalities that you've referred to as Plaski and Vrhovine were originally part of Korenica, Titova Korenica, is that -- is that -- am I clear on your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Those municipalities back in 1990 were within the framework of the neighbouring municipalities. Plaski of the municipality of Agolin [phoen] and Vrhovine was a part of the municipality of Obrovac, and on the basis of a referendum by the beginning of 1991 the Serb population of that area voted in favour of joining the neighbouring municipality of Korenica and so after the referendum they were included in the Titova Korenica municipality. But during the existence of the SAO Krajina, they again went independent and they set up separate municipalities, first Plaski and then later on Vrhovine as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, I can hear in my ear phones that the interpreter is having a little difficulty keeping up with you. You speak very fast. If you can just remember to speak a little bit more slowly, please. Now, do you know --

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know what the ethnic composition of Lika was in 1990-91?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: This -- in this territory that belonged to Krajina, the Serbs were 75 or -- between 75 and 80 per cent and the Croats were the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Let me ask you about the area called Kordun, referred to as Kordun. Which municipalities were in this area?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: There were the municipalities of Vrgin Most, Vojnic, Slunj, and Krnjak.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The first one is -- I could hear it but it didn't get captured. Was it Vrgin Most?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes, Vrginmost; it's single word.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And what were the other ones? Vojnic, Slunj, and what was the last one?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Krnjak.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, Krnjak, could you tell us what was this municipality? Was this another new municipality?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: In 1990, it was on the territory of the municipality of Karlovac and there again the Serb population on the basis of a referendum voted in favour of joining the municipality of Vojnic. So for a while they were a part of that municipality and then later on they set up a separate municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So to be clear, the -- Krnjak was originally a part of Karlovac?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What was the ethnic makeup, if you know, of the region of Kordun in 1990, 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: In this area, Serbs made up about 75 per cent of the population and the rest were Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Next I want to ask you about the area known as Banija. Which municipalities were included in Banija?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: The municipalities of Glina, Dvor Na Uni, Kostajnica, Petrinja or most of the municipality of Petrinja, and the municipality of Sisak Caprag.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What was the ethnic makeup of Banija in 1990-91?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Serbs made up between 75 and 80 per cent of the population and 20, 25 per cent of the population was Croat, roughly speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: We've also heard about an area referred to as eastern Slavonia Baranja and Western Srem. I'm not going to ask you what the municipalities were in this area but can you tell us if you know what the ethnic composition of that area was in 1990-91?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: According to my assessment, Serbs made up 50 per cent of the population, about half of the population, and the other half were Croats and others.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: With the assistance of the usher I would like to show the witness a map and it's actually a copy of map 3 with some markings on it. And when I've referred to map 3, just so the record is clear, that's map 3 from Exhibit 22. If that could be placed on the ELMO, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, this map has markings in pink pen and in blue -- light blue pen on it. Do you recognise those markings?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes. I drew that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you recall when you drew that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The witness draw that? Did he draw that?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That was his testimony, yes, that he drew that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, do you recall when you drew this, those lines?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, the day before maybe.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you tell us -- I'll just have a few questions about this map and I'm mindful -- I'm aware of the time, that we are almost at the break. The pink line, what does the pink line represent, approximately?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Roughly speaking, it is the demarcation between SAO Krajina and Croatia and the part of Western Slavonia and Croatia by the end of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And the blue lines that you made, the light blue lines, what do those lines represent?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Those are the lines indicating the regional borders within the SAO Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If you -- if the usher could give the witness a pen, and if you could mark a 1 just so this -- we are clear on these regions, the -- a 1 in the area that you've identified -- that you've drawn to be Northern Dalmatia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: A 2 for Lika?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: A 3 for Kordun?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And a 4 for Banija?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And these lines that you've drawn, both the pink line and the light blue lines, are these approximate lines?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: The pink one is an approximate line. The blue line is correct because I used the existing line separating the municipalities. So it's more accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, could this be admitted into evidence, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number 176, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And this is a convenient time. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Then we will take a short break and come back at 4.00. Is that right? 4.00, 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. If I may interrupt you before you proceed, Mr. Whiting, just one little point. It's been made known to the Bench that on Friday, there is a possibility that we could sit in the morning and then get a free afternoon. If the parties are so inclined, they can give us an advice and we can make the necessary arrangements.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: We are available to did that, Your Honour, just to be clear that would be -- we would sit in the morning and then we would not sit in the afternoon?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If that would be helpful to you, to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Then we will then sit in the morning on Friday. You may proceed, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, if I could turn your attention, please, to the map that is in front of you, and it -- the map that I'm referring to is 01131342, which I'm holding up, and for the purposes of the record, just to remind the Chamber that the translation of the front -- of the contents of the front of this map is in evidence as Exhibits 15 and 16, I won't ask that that be called up right now because I have a very brief question about it and it can be checked, looked at later if that's necessary. Mr. Babic, I want to draw your attention to the blue box in the lower right-hand corner of the map. Do you see that box?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you tell us what is contained in that box?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: The heading Krajina is in -- represented by numbers which represent regions of Krajina, indicating the surface area, the number of inhabitants, the ethnic makeup, how many Serbs, Croats, and others, according to regions and the SAO Krajina, Eastern and Western Slavonia, if that's what you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You testified before, I believe, that this map was prepared in 1993 or 1994. Do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, I just going to go briefly through the regions with you. Northern Dalmatia, what is reflected there as the Serb population, in terms of percentage? Can you find that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: 90 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Lika? Serb population?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: 93 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Kordun? Serb population?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: 98 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Banija? Serb population?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: 97 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, could this map and the back of the map with the translation be admitted into evidence, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The map and the back of the map, translation. Could the map and the translation relating to what was written on the back of the map are admitted into evidence. May they please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number 177 for the map and Exhibit number 178 for the translations, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And that can be taken away from the witness, thank you. I have no more questions about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, I want to talk about another topic now. I want to talk about your motivations for joining the SDS. You testified earlier today that you joined the SDS in February of 1990 and that you held various positions within the SDS. Can you tell the Chamber, why did you join the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: I was first of all interested in the development of the welfare in Knin, where I lived, and I felt that through this new political party I could make my own contribution in -- the Serb Democratic Party was a party which declared itself as democratic one, and was asking for changes in society. It was a democratic party which represented the Serb national interests in Croatia, and the Knin region had a majority of Serb population so my motive was threefold, in fact. A desire to make my contribution to development of the region, a desire to participate in the putting into practice of the programme and the manifesto of the Serb Democratic Party in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The third reason?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, Your Honour has asked what the third reason is. It appeared that you gave two reasons.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes. So the first reason, the development of the region; the second reason, because it was a national party; and the third reason because it was a party which was putting into practice democratic changes in society.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You testified that the party represented the Serb national interests in Croatia. Could you tell us what those were or how those were interpreted by the party? What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: The Serb people in Croatia was a constituent people according to Croatian constitution but they were still a minority of the population of the Republic of Croatia. So the national interest was the protection of the cultural identity of the Serb people and the economic prosperity of those areas inhabited by Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you tell us what some of the concerns were of Serbs that -- at that time, that you were aware of?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Well, the Serbs were concerned on both counts that I've just mentioned. Even before the setting up of the new government in Croatia, even back in 1989, and especially at the start of the 1990s or in 1990, national and nationalist political organisations were on the rise in Croatia and their approach to the internal setup of Croatia was different. They felt that Croatian culture and language should be upgraded and that the Serb people in Croatia should no longer be a constituent people but just a national minority.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You've started to answer this question but maybe you can elaborate a little further. Could you describe for us in general terms, at this point, what the differences were between the different political approaches or different political parties that existed in Croatia in 1990?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: The main political party in Croatia was the HDZ, which won the first multi-party democratic elections. The election campaign of that party was very clear. Members of the party and more specifically the president of the party who later on went on to become the president of Croatia promoted those policies. They advocated the creation of a Greater Croatia in the area of the then Republic of Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina and they were in favour of Croatia becoming independent and separating from the former Yugoslavia, and that policy was supported by some other national and nationalist parties. On the Serb side, the main party, the most influence party, was the SDS, which represented a political approach according to which it would be a good idea to stick to the Yugoslav federation and that there should be autonomous regions within Croatia in those areas in which the Serb population were in the majority, and they were in favour of a democrat transformation of society. Actually all parties were in favour of that if we think in terms of getting rid of the old communist system. All of them except for the Communist League movement for Yugoslavia, which only seemed to have any impact amongst the JNA members in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Was there conflict between these two broad approaches, that is the approach of the HDZ and the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes. Absolutely. There was a political conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did this --

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Which --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I think I -- I didn't mean to cut you off. You were -- did you want to finish your answer? You said there was a political conflict which --

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes. That political conflict had already started by explaining the political programmes before the elections and continued after the elections when the HDZ came to power and the SDS came to power in some mostly Serb municipalities within Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In time, did this conflict escalate?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: It did escalate. Politically speaking, as well as in terms of violence and demonstrations of force, and in the end it was an all-out war during 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, you said in your answer that it escalated both politically speaking and in terms of violence and demonstrations of force. Could you tell us, please, was one side responsible for the escalation in terms of violence and demonstrations of force?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Both sides were responsible, but to my knowledge, the Serb side began using force first.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Was the SDS party formed anywhere else besides in the Krajina region of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: The SDS under that name was formed for the region of -- for the area of Croatia, but it wanted to be organised in the entire former Yugoslavia. Therefore they organised some of their boards in Serbia and in the Bosnian Krajina. That is the SDS often referred to as the SDS-Croatia, although its name was only SDS, and its president was Dr. Raskovic. Under the name of the SDS, there were some other parties formed elsewhere. For example, we had the SDS of Bosnia-Herzegovina as a separate party, and by the end of 1990, some SDS boards in Serbia formed their own SDS of Serbia. That was the situation back in 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You said that the -- you made reference to the SDS of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Who was the leader of that party?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Dr. Radovan Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You said a moment ago that to your knowledge, the Serb side began using force first. When did that occur, approximately?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: It occurred on the 17th of August 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'll ask you more questions about that later. Could you tell us, Mr. Babic, when did you first meet Milan Martic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: I first met him in July 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What was the circumstance of meeting him?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: At the time, Mr. Martic was employed with the police station in Knin, and together with a group of other policemen, initiated a signing of a petition among the policemen against the introduction of new Croatian symbols as well as new uniforms and the change of name for the members of the police in Croatia. In that protest he referred to Dr. Raskovic, that is he went to see him and Dr. Raskovic advised him to go and see me. And that's how we met.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: This Dr. Raskovic is that the same Dr. Raskovic that you identified a moment ago as being the president of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And what happened in the meeting that you had with Mr. Martic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: I thought it would be all right to see him and the.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not understand the meaning of Mr. Babic's words but he said that I thought he was correct, it was the right thing to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I think the interpreter had a little difficulty understanding your last answer. Can you repeat it, if you recall it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: I received information from Mr. Martic that they put together a text for the petition, sent it to federal Minister of the Interior, and that they wanted to see that published in the media. I believe they called it the petition.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Who was the federal Minister of the Interior at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Petar Gracanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Was there subsequently a meeting with Croatian officials?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes. After that, a delegation from the Croatian Ministry of the Interior came to the police station in Knin to try and deal with the situation. That is to try to force those policemen who signed the petition to express their loyalty to the newly formed state.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you recall who was in this delegation?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: I forgot their names. There was an assistant Minister of the Interior and an undersecretary, a younger man, and the rumour had it that he came back from abroad and that he was at that time employed with the Ministry of Interior in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you recall when this meeting occurred?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: In July of 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Were you present at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you tell us what happened?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: We had a discussion during the meeting and we heard explanations from both parties. The Knin policemen expressed their reasons for signing, and the Zagreb delegation expressed theirs. And during the meeting, a lot of people assembled in front of the police station from Knin and the surrounding settlements, because by that time, people heard that there were Croatian Special Forces deployed to one of the nearby forests. That's why the tension increased. And we had to think of a way for the delegation to leave safely. A few of us tried to convince those people to move elsewhere, to make it possible for the delegation to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, was Mr. Martic present at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you recall what his role was?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: I don't remember anything in particular. There was discussion and the policemen stated their views as well as the ministry delegation from Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you give a speech on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: I believe I spoke at the station. I can't remember precisely but I do know that I tried to speak with the people assembled in front of the station to break up.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did Mr. Martic, do you recall whether he -- him making any kind of a speech on this occasion or afterwards?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: I don't remember him speaking during the meeting, but I think he did give some statements to the press and the television.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you remember the content of those statements?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: The most famous of his sentences was that the Croatian coat of arms will not be seen on the Knin fort for as long as he lived. That's what made his famous throughout the Krajina. He became a national hero.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You made a reference to the Knin fort. What is the Knin fort?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: It's a fortress, a mediaeval fortress which used to be the city of Knin, and there are some apartments there, various restaurants, the Chamber of commerce at the time was there and it's up on a hill overlooking the city.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is the fort a suburb in Knin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is in the centre. It is both the centre and the suburbs because at the same time that's where the town ends because there is the river on the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Does the fort have any symbolic significance?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Please tell us.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: It has symbolic value as the city centre, as well as a military stronghold taken over by the Serb soldiers from the Turks for the Republic of Venice. Therefore it has a historical importance as well as the symbolical importance for the survival of Serbs in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you have another meeting with Mr. Martic in August of 1990?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Around the 10th or a day before the 10th of August 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What happened on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: I was in the neighbourhood seeing one of the neighbours for an afternoon coffee. I was there with my family and a friend. And Mr. Martic walked into the house wearing a combat uniform and a rifle. That was a military uniform.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: A police uniform.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He said, stay calm, everything is fine. But the Croatian Special Forces have been sent to attack us, to attack Krajina. We didn't remain calm, of course. We were quite upset. And he said that I should leave with my family that night. One of the people who was with him, Mr. Pepina Cupkovic took me and my family to a house where we spent the night, allegedly to be protected from the Croatian Special Forces who tried to enter Knin. But on that day, there were none. In the morning we were told by several people that we were supposed to go to see Slobodan Milosevic to seek protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'll ask you about that in a moment but first I want to ask you about the uniform that you said Mr. Martic was wearing. You described it both as a combat uniform and a police uniform. Could you explain that, please?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: As a uniform worn by policemen when they have to be deployed. They have a cap, a rifle, and boots. That would be as far as the difference goes concerning their standard uniform in peacetime, when they only carry a gun, a pistol.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And the uniform, could you just describe the colour of it, please?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: A blue police uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You said that the following day you were told by several people that you were supposed to go see Slobodan Milosevic. Do you recall who told you that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: I believe I was told that by Mr. Martic. I can't recall his words precisely, but David Rastovic was there who was the president of the Donji Lapac municipality and the vice-president of the Serb National Council, and Mr. Popovic of Zadar, a retired colonel and a vice-president of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you go -- did you meet with Slobodan Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes. Indirectly, the next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Explain what you mean by that.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: I learned that President Milosevic was at Kupari close to Dubrovnik on his vacation and that I should contact members of the Presidency. Mr. Slobodan Vucetic, among others, who at the time was in Bilovci [phoen] in Montenegro. I was told to speak with the Slobodan Vucetic to establish communication with Slobodan Milosevic at Kupari. I did so. I went to Kupari with Mr. Vucetic but I stayed outside next to the road. And Mr. Vucetic entered the military facility compound, that's where military officers could go for their vacation, and he passed on the information to Mr. Slobodan Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you find out who Mr. Milosevic was there with?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vucetic said all three of them are there. He said that with Milosevic there were the president of the SFRY Presidency, Mr. Jovic, and the Federal Defence Secretary, Mr. Kadijevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You identified Mr. Jovic as being the president of the SFRY Presidency. From which republic was Mr. Jovic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: From Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know what his relationship was at the time to Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: He was a member of the Socialist Party of Serbia, the president being Mr. Milosevic. He was one of Milosevic's men within the federal bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Why did you want to meet with Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: To seek protection in Serbia, and to have a channel for the Serbs in Croatia to express the difficulties they have been experiencing with the new Croatian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Why go to Mr. Milosevic to get protection? Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
