utterances.text: Milosevic was the then Serbian president, and his party, as well as himself personally, were for the unified Yugoslavia encompassing all the Serb territories and all the Serb population. He was presenting himself as the protector of Serbs throughout Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You told us that your message was taken to Mr. Milosevic by Mr. Vucetic, but what happened next? What's the next thing that happened?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Milosevic said that we should ask for an official meeting with President Jovic and that we express our concerns to him and to go to attend a meeting in Belgrade, inside the federation palace.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you do that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes. We sent an official request for Mr. Jovic to see us, and so he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you recall when that occurred?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: It was, I believe, on the 13th of August, that is two days after the meeting with Milosevic. Or three, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What happened at that meeting? What did you say; what did Mr. Jovic say?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: I explained the political situation of the Serbs in Croatia, and the constitutional changes made by the new Croatian authorities. They wanted to abolish the rights of the Serbs as a constituent people. I also explained that we were in preparations to hold a referendum for the Serbs in Croatia, and the other members of the delegation explained the threats made for an armed intervention, the threats being made by the then Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Croatia. That's what we told Jovic more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And what did he say to you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: He explained that they were preparing a draft law on secession, to be put before the federal assembly. He said that he supported our political struggle and that the JNA will serve as a guarantee of that struggle and support as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That last part, that the JNA will serve as a guarantee of that struggle and support as well, on subsequent occasions, did others tell you that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was one of basic tenets of Milosevic. During any meeting with Milosevic, whether it was myself or someone else, he kept saying that the JNA would protect us. He repeated that often.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And when it's us, the JNA would protect us, who was he referring to?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: The Serbs in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In -- when is the first time you met with Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: We met face to face in October 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: From that time until the end of 1991, approximately how many times did you meet with Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Around 20 times.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The meeting that you were describing for us with Mr. Jovic, were you with -- did anybody else -- did anybody go with you to that meeting, from Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: I was there, then David Rastovic [Realtime transcript read in error "Raskovic"] and Bogoljub Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did they speak about anything?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: I would just like to make a correction to the transcript. It is not Raskovic but Rastovic and Bogoljub Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you for that because we have Jovan Rastovic and -- I'm sorry, now I've made the mistake. Jovan Raskovic and David Rastovic, and those are two different people, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes. Jovan Raskovic was the president of the SDS and Mr. Rastovic was the vice-president of the Serbian National Council and the president of the municipality of Donji Lapac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, if we could go back to my question, did David Rastovic or Bogoljub Popovic say anything at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes. As I said already, we each had our own share of discussion. I explained the political difficulties and the situation with the Serbs in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you meet with anybody else on that trip to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: After the meeting with Jovic we met with the federal Minister of the Interior, Mr. Petar Gracanin. When leaving the meeting with Jovic we spoke with an adviser of his, I believe, one of his staff within the cabinet. He said precisely in what way we needed to hold a referendum. He stated that we should put it into law and to harmonise it with the constitutions of Yugoslavia and Croatia, to include the category of self declaration.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In your meeting with Mr. Gracanin, the federal Minister of the Interior, what was discussed?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: More or less the same as with Mr. Jovic, but from the security standpoint. For example, about what was going on within the Croatian police, what was the reaction of the Ministry of the Interior of Croatia concerning the events in Knin, as well as the referendum to be held and the situation with the police in Knin itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did Mr. Gracanin later talk about this meeting in the media?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes. He said that he suggested to the Serbs to put barricades on roads. I don't remember that he said that precisely but I believe he also met with a police delegation prior, although I'm uncertain of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What happened after you returned to Croatia from this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: We held a meeting of the Serbian National Council at Dvor Na Uni to have a clear standpoint as to the Serbs in Croatia declaring themselves independent.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we publish, please, 65 ter number 33? Is it necessary to have the ERN? No? Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On page 55 -- no, page 50, line 7, 16:08:16 there is a mistranslation of the reply supplied by the witness as to what was agreed at the meeting when he came back from Belgrade. I wouldn't like to comment on it now so perhaps if you could ask the witness once again? Because it says that it was agreed that Serbs in Croatia should ask for independence and the witness did not mention that. He simply referred to the fact that the citizens should declare themselves and he never mentioned independence at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll try to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, could you tell us -- there has been perhaps a little problem with the translation. Could you tell us again what happened with this meeting when you returned from Belgrade to Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: We had a meeting of the Serb National Council at Dvor Na Uni. At that meeting, it was decided that we would survey the Serb people in Croatia asking them about the Serb autonomy.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I think that clarifies the issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, if you could -- if we could turn to page 2 of that document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, can you read that on the screen? Do you see a document in front of you, a handwritten document on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes. These are the minutes from the meeting that was held on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And on which day?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: The 16th of August 1999 -- 1990, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know who wrote these minutes?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: I think the Secretary of the Serb National Council, Mr. Vjestica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What is his first name, Mr. Vjestica's first name?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Dusan Vjestica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Have you seen these minutes before?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes. I submitted it to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Are they accurate minutes of the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I want to look down, if we could scroll down further, further, there. Thank you. There, there, there. Do you see where it says, Jovic gave support to all political battles? No, no. I can't tell if that's --

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you just read that sentence, please?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: The sentence reads as follows: "Jovic gave his support to all political battles for the rights of the peoples and for the referendum to be carried out according to the legal provisions, and he said that the army would give their support and protection and grant protection to the political struggle of the Serb people. The attitude --"

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's fine. Thank you. And then do you see where it says, "Rastovic" and it's underlined? Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And what does it say after that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: "The guarantor of what we declare is the army."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, could this be moved into evidence, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence and may it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number 179, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, this was on the 16th of August 1990. What happened on the following day, on the 17th of August 1990? Before I ask you that, I have another question to ask you. You told us that before you went to Belgrade, Mr. Martic appeared in a combat uniform and said that -- to tell you that the Croatian Special Forces were arriving. Did that ever occur? Did they ever arrive?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: No, not at the time. There were conflicts later but not then. And not on the following day either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have something to complain about in the transcript once again. It's line 18. By way of reply, it says the army will provide guarantees for whatever we declare, and the witness never mentioned it. So the witness was reading out the text from this handwritten document which seems to be saying something else, at least as far as my understanding goes, so could we perhaps rectify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, we are looking at the English translation and when I looked at this translation, it seems to me as if the witness said it exactly as it stood on the English translation. But you can help us because we don't understand B/C/S. If the English translation is not exactly the same as the B/C/S version ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think Your Honour is correct that the witness was at that point simply reading from the document and that the -- what he read and the way it was translated here is in essence the same as has been translated in the official translation of the document. So I'm not clear on what the problem is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the text that was submitted to the witness is a handwritten text, and it includes a statement according to which the army - and I'm paraphrasing it now - will be a guarantor in case a political statement is made by the population as to their destiny and here it says that they would be guarantor for the decision made, which is somewhat different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, maybe we must give the B/C/S document to one of the interpreters to interpret to us in English, because as I say, I looked at the English version and the -- what was translated to me was the exactly the same as or substantially the same as what was on the document before me, which is an English version. Is it possible for one of the translators -- interpreters to please help us?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may on this, the document, of course, has already been translated and the translation is now in evidence. If counsel has an issue about the way it's been translated, it seems to me that that could be raised at another time and we could resolve it at another time, and we could continue with the witness. The witness was merely reading out what's in the document so there is nothing coming from the witness himself on this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milovancevic? You have to -- do you want to say something, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe that we could solve this issue if we could show this sentence to the witness once again and if we could reread it perhaps, because all I'm saying is that the witness did not actually make any comment of his own. He just read out a phrase that was in these minutes. So if he could just read it once again, it may be something we can argue with or not, but if the witness could read it out once again, and then we could know for sure because what you've got is a translation into English and then it has been re-translated and changed again through the witness's response, and I believe if the witness could be shown this same phrase once again and if he could read it out once again we could solve the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But, Mr. Milovancevic, you've just told me now that the witness read it without comment, and what was translated as what he read was substantially the same as what I saw on the screen in the English version. So why do you want him to read it again? You want him to read it with a comment?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. No, Your Honour. What the witness has read out has been mistranslated. That's the essence of my comment. It is totally different from what is in the transcript so could the witness reread the sentence and then we can make a comparison once again? That's what I was going to suggest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Babic would you please read that sentence again? I hope you do know which sentence this is. This I suppose was the sentence -- okay. Let me not get into it. Read the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do know. Yes. It says, "Raskovic," underlined, and then -- and then his words, "the guarantor of our declaration is army -- is the army."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. I can tell you now, Mr. Milovancevic that's what's written in the English here is "the army is the guarantee for our declaration," and I'm reading it as is without correction. "Guarantee."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you. May I proceed, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, this meeting occurred on the 16th of August 1990. What occurred on the following day, on the 17th of August?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: On the 17th of August, several events took place, or rather there was unrest in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you elaborate a little bit? What kind of unrest? What happened precisely?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Well, perhaps I could give you a description of the events. Perhaps that would be best.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That would be --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: My microphone seems to be having problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That would be perfect if you gave us a description of the events.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: On the 17th of August, the municipal assembly, I received a telex message from Sergej Veselinovic, the president of the municipality of Obrovac, saying that the special forces from Croatia --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, if you don't mind, don't go too fast so the interpreters can keep up. I'm sorry to interrupt you. Please continue and I hope I didn't interrupt your train of thought there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I may just say before you carry on, Mr. Babic, if you can say short sentences, give the interpreter an opportunity to interpret, and then go on again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you. On the 17th of August, 1990, I was at the office of the municipal assembly in Knin. That's where I received a telex message from the president of the municipality of Obrovac, Sergej Veselinovic. The message said that Croatian Special Forces set out to attack Obrovac and the area of Knin and that they were setting up barricades on Velebit. At the same time, or a couple of minutes later, Dusan Orlovic came to see me. A man who had close ties to Mr. Martic and the police movement. And afterwards he was an aide to the Interior Secretary and the Secretary in charge of Internal Security. He told me that Croatian armoured transport vehicles were entering Knin, and he was rather agitated. That's at least the way he came across. And so I believed him. And I ordered some of my staff to sound the sirens from the municipality, from the town hall, that is. And I went to the village called Strmica and I told one of the men who was accompanying me to declare a state of emergency in town, and then I said, perhaps a state of war, rather. And so he conveyed that message or something along these lines, and the message -- I don't really know in what way but at any rate, it somehow got to the Tanjug news agency for Croatia and it was reported in the media that the president of the municipality of Knin, Milan Babic, had declared a state of war in Knin, and people got really nervous and there was a lot of traffic jams on the roads in Croatia. It was a tourist season and I stayed for a while in that village and since nothing happened I went to the centre at Golubic. It was where some youth-work actions used to take place and I wanted to ask Mr. Martic and Orlovic what was going on, and then they said that there were no Croatian Special Forces, that they were not on their way to Knin but at that time we were -- they were busy distributing the weapons from the police reserve forces to the people who were there. And so I was slightly embarrassed and I went back to town and I basically took my words back and I said that there was no state of war, but as of then, barricades started to go up all over the place in Knin, Gracac, Lapac, Obrovac, in the area of Lika and Dalmatia, and so that was the start of what the Croat press called the "Balvan revolution." Afterwards, the staff for barricades was set up in Golubic, and Mr. Martic and another group of people from the SDS were in charge of that, and the staff was set up on the basis of a decision of the main board of the SDS. But actually it only functioned for a couple of days, maybe two or three weeks at the most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I interrupt you. I'm sorry, Mr. Babic, to do this to you. A number of questions arise from this long answer and I would like to get, to follow your answer. Who distributed these weapons? You said that Mr. Martic and somebody else told you that there were no Special Forces coming but that they were busy distributing weapons from the police reserve forces to the people who were there. Is it Mr. Martic who distributed the weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And who had sent the telex that you first received before -- right at the beginning of this long answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sergej Veselinovic, the president of the municipality of Obrovac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, I also have some questions about that long answer. You mentioned Dusan Orlovic. What was his position at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: At the time he was a close ally of Mr. Martic but he was a civilian.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And what position -- you made reference to a position that he held later on. Could you explain what position he held later on?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: For a long time, he was an aide to the Secretary of the Interior and Security, and later on he was an aide to the Minister of the Interior for state security, in both instances in Krajina, and after 1995 he was again an employee of the state security service in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When he was an aide to the Secretary of the Interior, who was the Secretary of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milan Martic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And when he was an aide to the Minister of the Interior for State Security, who was the Minister of the Interior then?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milan Martic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Was he in charge of state security?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: I don't understand. Who do you mean, "was he in charge."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you. That was a good question. Was Mr. Orlovic in charge of state security?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: He was for a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And was state security within the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: There will be more questions on this later. You said that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I may just ask one more question.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry. On this occasion, what position did Mr. Milan Martic hold?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean on the 17th of August? Well, informally he was the head or the leader of the police uprising in Knin. I'm talking about the 17th of August here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: He -- right. That's a self-appointed position, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was the leader of the movement in question. So -- well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But within the police, did he hold any official position also?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the time, he was an inspector at the police station in Knin. I believe that's the correct terminology.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And state security is referred to sometimes by -- is it referred to sometimes by an abbreviation?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes, DB.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, you --

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Or SDB, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sometimes DB, sometimes SDB?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes, mostly DB. That's the shortest way.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you referred -- you referred to seeing Milan Martic in Golubic and you asked about where these Croatian Special Forces were and they said they weren't coming. Did the Croatian Special Forces ever appear, that is on that day?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Not on that day, as far as I know. On that day, Croatian police from Zagreb set out for Knin in a helicopter. That's something that I found out at a later stage but they -- then the JNA air force intervened and they were sent back to Zagreb so they didn't get to Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You also made reference to barricades that went up, and what was the name that the Croatian press started to call this?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: I've already mentioned it, "Balvan revolution," log revolution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you. And what was Milan Martic's role in the erecting of the barricades?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: At first, he was the head of the barricade staff, and there upon he was the leader of the illegal organisation which was called the council of international -- of national resistance against the putting down of Serbs or something like that. And they were in charge of the barricades. Basically they were known as the council of national resistance and then it was officially taken over by the Secretariat for the Interior of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to ask some questions to try to be a little bit more detailed and specific about what you've just told us. Before you started to tell us about what happened in Golubic in the days after August 17th, can you tell us again what -- what happened there in Golubic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: What particular point in time do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: After -- after August 17th.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes. Golubic or rather this youth camp was turned into a military camp, with guards at the entry gates, armed individuals. It was a military camp, the way I saw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And what function did the military camp have, if any?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: It represented the staff and the gathering point for those who were in charge of the barricades, who took part in this uprising. It was supposed to be a place from where the barricades would be managed but it turned into something resembling a military camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Who was in charge there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Milan Martic was in charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How long did the camp exist there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Not very long, maybe two to three weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What happened then?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Since I noticed that it was no longer a barricades staff but actually a military camp which was rather dangerous, considering the political situation at the time and the political attitude represented by the SDS at the time, I told that much to Mr. Raskovic, the president of the party, and I asked him to convene a meeting of the party board and to require that military camp to be disbanded and that it should not be within the area of responsibility of the SDS because it was compromising the SDS position and policy and that was the decision that was made and the military camp and the staff were both disbanded.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What happened next?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: The people from the staff or the camp or Mr. Martic, that is, simply moved to another location on the outskirts of Golubic, afterwards, the village of Otun [phoen], afterwards a part of Knin which is called Sinobadova Glavica, but it was no longer the barricade staff. But it was actually something that was presented to the general public as the Council of National Resistance but they acted as an illegal organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, I'll ask you some more questions about the Council of National Resistance but I think we've reached a time for the next break. And I learned from the last time that if I go over, it's deducted from the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Court adjourned. We will come back at quarter to six.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, before the break, you talked about -- you started to talk about the Council of National Resistance which you said acted as an illegal organisation, and earlier you provided a little bit of information about it. But could you tell us now what did the Council of National Resistance do in the fall of 1990?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: The Council of National Resistance appeared after the 10th of September 1992 [as interpreted]. That is, after the negotiations in which several presidents of municipalities of the Serb Krajina had with the representatives of the Croatian parliament and we arranged for a situation to be normalised in Croatia. The Council of National Resistance appeared as the enemy of easing the tensions and against the agreement reached with the Croatian authorities, and they also had their own view of the way negotiations should be conducted and future problems resolved. The Council of National Resistance actually provoked, they elevated tension by way of issuing dramatic statements and announcements via the media. They also blocked rail traffic, they mined tunnels, they blew up kiosks and private shops owned by Croats. They even planned to cut off electricity for Knin, to create as much tension as possible, and to provoke an intervention by the JNA and the introduction of the state of emergency in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, in the beginning of that answer, the interpretation we got is that you said that the Council of National Resistance appeared after the 10th of September 1992. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you. Why did the Council of National Resistance want to provoke intervention by the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: In order to further the policies represented by Milosevic and Jovic. They were in favour of the state of emergency in Croatia and they wanted to see the Croatian government fall and they wanted to introduce the military -- to install the military administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And when you say to further the policies represented by Milosevic and Jovic, what policies are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to the policy of creation of a state to encompass all of the Serbs in Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina as well by way of taking over Serb territories and for the others to leave Yugoslavia if they chose to. That was the essence of their policy.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'll ask you some more questions about that later. You've already identified the role that Milan Martic played in the Council of National Resistance. Who else, if you know, was involved in that organisation?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: That organisation never published a list of its members or its structure. It functioned illegally and what one could observe in Knin, the organisation encompassed people from the police, some citizens, a part of the SDS membership, then Jovo Vitas, Dusan Orlovic, Nebojsa Magdinic [phoen] was an official of Knin municipality. Then Nebojsa, aka Neso Maric. I can't remember any other names.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Jovo Vitas, who was he? What position did he hold at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Jovo Vitas was a trader, a private entrepreneur in Knin. As for the Council of National Resistance, he often had communiques.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter missed a part of the witness's question. Could he please repeat?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, you may have to speak a little -- up a little bit. The interpreter missed the last part of your answer. Could you repeat that answer about Jovo Vitas?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Jovo Vitas was a trader in Knin, a private entrepreneur, a citizen of Knin. As for the Council of National Defence, he often had their communiques and would deliver them to the radio, and he often transported explosives from the police station in Knin to the barricades. He often was with the centre for sounding alarm in -- with the municipal assembly, and he seemed to be a very mobile person, multi-tasks within the council. He even threatened to kill me after I signed agreement with the -- Mr. Boljkovac and Mr. Degoricija from the Croatian parliament concerning a peaceful resolution for the situation in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Around the 10th of September 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You said that he often transported explosives from the police station in Knin to the barricades. How did you know that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: I saw him load explosives and he was driving that vehicle. People were talking about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You also mentioned Neso Maric. Who was he?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: He was a guy from Knin. I don't know what his occupation was. But he was quite close to Milan Martic. He was often seen as his escort.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When did he -- when was he the escort for Milan Martic? During what period of time, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: From that time until 1995, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And what did he do, if you know, as the escort for Milan Martic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Personal guard.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, you've made reference to this event on the 10th of September 1990. Could you explain, please, for the Court what occurred then?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Upon the initiative of the president of the Sinj municipal assembly, who was a member of the HDZ, the leading party in Croatia at the time, to meet with me. I agreed and we discussed several items, among other how to resolve the problems existing between the municipalities of Knin and Sinj, in particular concerning the supply of electricity and water since these were often cut off due to the barricades and the conflict. We also discussed holding a meeting in Donji Lapac between the representatives of the Serbian municipalities and the government, i.e., the parliament and the Ministry of the Interior of Croatia concerning a resolution for the -- to the crisis. We also discussed my visit to President Tudjman in Zagreb. On the 10th of September, a meeting was held indeed in Donji Lapac. On the Croatian side there were the president of the assembly of municipalities, Mr. Slavko Degoricija, Minister of the Interior Mr. Boljkovac, and an official of the Minister of the Interior. On the Serb side -- there was Jerko Vukas as part of their delegation as well. On the Serb side, I was there, then the president of municipality of Donji Lapac, the Secretary of the Serb National Council, Mr. Dusan Vjestica, the president of the Executive Council of Donji Lapac, Mr. Djukic, who was also -- and the secretary of the municipality in Donji Lapac. We made an agreement there to peacefully resolve the outstanding issues and to return the weapons taken from the reserve police forces and stations. Those weapons were taken in August that year. We also agreed that there be an initiative to form a Secretariat of the Interior within the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Croatia with its seat in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter Exhibit number 34, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And while that is being brought up on the screen, Mr. Babic, with respect to that last -- the last part of your answer, the initiative to form a Secretariat of the Interior within the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Croatia with its seat in Knin, would that Secretariat be subordinated to the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Croatia, that is would it still be within that ministry or would it be separate?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: It would be still within the Ministry of the Interior, as its branch office, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, can you see the document in front of you? Is that -- on our monitor it's not in B/C/S. It's not particularly clear but --

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you recognise that document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was the communique issued after the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: After the meeting on the 10th of September 1990?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you provide this document to the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could this be admitted into evidence, please, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number 180, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, what was the reaction of the Council of National Resistance to this initiative that you participated in?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: On that same evening or the next day, they found me at the centre for sounding the alarm by two members of the council and I was threatened by them; they said I should be killed, as a traitor. The weapons were not returned, however. In that way, they undermined the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The weapons that were distributed in Golubic on the 17th of August 1990, were they ever returned?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: A part of the weapons was returned in January 1990, upon the SFRY Presidency request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Excuse me, there is something wrong there. You're asking about the weapons that were distributed on the 17th of August. The answer is that they were returned on the -- in January of the same year.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'll try to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When -- can you tell us again when a part of the weapons were returned?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: In January next year, that is 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the barricades that were erected starting on the 17th of August 1991, how long did they stay in place?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: They stayed in place for as long as the frontline was established, the line that separated the armed forces of the Krajina and the JNA on one side, and on the other side the Croat forces. That is approximately until April 1991, until that time those were barricades and after that it was the active line of defence as well as the starting point for any attacks against Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And after August of -- after the log revolution began on the 17th of August 1990, what was Milan Martic's reputation?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: For the public, he was a Serb national hero, the leader of resistance against the Croat authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Which public?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: The Serb public.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: During the rest of 1990 and into 1991, could you tell us what the nature of your relationship was with Mr. Martic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Formally speaking, the relationship was established as of January 1991 when the interim Executive Council of the SAO Krajina elected Milan Martic as Secretary of the Interior. Later on, he became Minister of the Interior of the SAO Krajina and the RSK, and president of the RSK, the Republic of the RSK.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: During 1991, then, you were -- you were president in various capacities and he was either a secretary or a minister. Was he -- was Milan Martic under your control?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Because Milan Martic belonged to the parallel structures in Krajina. He was controlled by the DBA of Serbia and Slobodan Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you explain for us a little bit more what you mean by the parallel structures? What does that mean? And you said controlled by the what of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: When I say parallel structures, I mean the hierarchy of power and force, so to speak, within the SAO Krajina, established by the members of the Ministry of the Interior of Serbia, plus members of the State Security of Serbia, some members of the SDS, some members of the police in the Serb municipalities in Krajina, and they represented parallel bodies to the legally elected authorities in Krajina, including the president and the assembly. That parallel structure was run by the State Security in Serbia and Slobodan Milosevic himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What was Milan Martic's role in the parallel structure?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: He was the most powerful man within the structure in the SAO Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Who within the Ministry of the Interior in Serbia or the DB of Serbia was -- participated in the parallel structure?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Radmilo Bogdanovic, Jovica Stanisic, Frenki Simatovic, Captain Dragan, that is Dragan Vasiljkovic. And they were assisted by some other people, in particular by Minister Sokolovic as well as some other people whose names I can't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Was the DB of Serbia within the Ministry of Interior of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Radmilo Bogdanovic, what was his role? What was his position, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Radmilo Bogdanovic was the secretary or the Minister of the Interior, as referred to the government of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter missed a date.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Until March 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And who was the Minister of Interior after March of 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Zoran Sokolovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Jovica Stanisic, what was his position?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: During 1991 and at the beginning of -- during 1990 and at the beginning of 1991 he was an employee of the state security service in Serbia. By the spring of 1991 he became the head of the State Security within the Ministry of the Interior of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And Frenki Simatovic, do you know his position?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Frenki Simatovic was an employee of the Serbian State Security Service and the head of one of its directorates. I believe he was the second directorate.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And finally Captain Dragan or Dragan Vasilkovic, what was his position?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Captain Dragan was a State Security Service employee or a contractor. His role was to be training instructor for the Special Forces of the police in Krajina, and he also commanded over one of the State Security Service's units.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: From April 1991 onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'll ask you more questions about all of these individuals later. But now I want to go back to your particular relationship with Mr. Martic. Were you able to give orders to Mr. Martic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you have any control over the police?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: No, I did not, because Martic obeyed the people from the parallel structure, that is Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Milosevic. He was supported by them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did Mr. Martic have control over the police?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: We've heard about the TO. Did you have control over the TO in the SAO Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Based on the law on Krajina, I was the Supreme Commander of the TO.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That was based on the law. Did you have any real authority over the TO?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: No, I did not, in any command sense of the word.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you describe for the Court the command structure of the TO after January of 1991, within the SAO Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: The TO in the area of the SAO Krajina was organised into municipal staffs and the TO units. The -- those staffs and units were supposed to have been commanded by the TO staff in Zagreb, but since Krajina seceded from the rest of Croatia until March 1991, the TO for Krajina was not linked up. As from August 1991, when the assembly based on the decision adopted the law or rather implemented the law of the National Defence in Serbia in the territory of Krajina, that is when the networking of the staffs and units of TO began. Hence, trying to make a unified structure for the TO in the region of Krajina. By the end of September 1991, the Main Staff of the TO was formed, as well as the zone staffs of TO of Krajina. By early October the unification of the TO for Krajina was complete.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: From January of 1991 until August of 1991, did -- did any TO units exist?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: There were just municipal staffs and units either existed only on paper or did not exist at all, as far as I know. The -- there were plans for such units to exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What happened to the individuals who comprised the units before January 1991, within the SAO Krajina? What happened to those people?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: They were not permanent units because the system of the people's Defence in the Socialist Federative Republic of former Yugoslavia had two components, an active component, that is to say the JNA, and Defence, Territorial Defence component which is made up of the TO units and they were set up only under conditions characterised by an imminent danger of war. The only parts of the TO that were constantly in operation were the staffs, and that at different levels, the republic level, the local level, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So -- Mr. Babic, did you hear that His Honour's words that just slow down a little bit? It's -- so during this phase from January of 1991 to August of 1991, what armed units existed within the SAO Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: The militia of Krajina and voluntary units.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The volunteer units were under whose control?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Under the control of the police or rather the parallel structure of state security.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you have any control over armed units during this period, January 1991 to August of 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In August of 1991, when the TO structure was organised, were there TO units then in existence?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's when they started setting up the TO units, as well as the volunteer units. I mean, they were also being turned into TO units.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And after August of 1991, who commanded these TO units and volunteer units?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: In the SAO Krajina, it was the commander of the TO, Milan Martic, or else the relevant JNA commander on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When was Milan Martic the commander of the TO?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Starting the 8th of August 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Until when?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Until the 30th of September 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What was his formal position during that time, with respect to the TO?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: He was the deputy commander of the TO.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If he was the deputy, who was the commander?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: I, as the head of government, was the commander of the TO.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you explain, then, why, if you were the commander and he was the deputy commander, you said that he commanded the TO units during this time period?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Well, because Slobodan Milosevic asked for him to become commander of the TO and since people from the parallel structures and from the JNA were under Milosevic's influence, that was the way in which his influence would also be felt, through Milan Martic. Actually, Slobodan Milosevic asked me to appoint Martic as commander of the TO, which I did not do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: During that time period, 8th of August to 30th of September 1991, did you give any orders to Milan Martic with respect to the TO?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: The only thing was my orders about the setting up of units and staffs. That's what we -- what was forwarded to him from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And were those orders taken or issued on your initiative or on somebody else's initiative?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Well, as to appointments, setting up of staffs, at the beginning of the setting up of the TO it was my initiative, with regard to the appointments of certain people within those staffs, but it didn't work. Up until the JNA or rather the headquarters back in Belgrade and Milosevic approved certain people to be appointed for certain positions within those staffs, that's when it started to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: After the 30th of September 1991, who commanded the TO units?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: There was the Main Staff of the Territorial Defence and regional staffs, which were of course under the command of the higher echelons of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I want to go back to -- and what was -- let me ask this first: What was Milan Martic's role then?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Milan Martic left the -- that position in a huff so to say because he was unhappy with the appointments for the new Main Staff because up until that very moment he was expecting to get the formal appointment as the commander of the TO, and it was at that moment that he withdrew from the fort and he went back to the police station in Knin, and that's where he acted as the Minister of the Interior for the SAO Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did he remain in command at that time of police forces?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I want to go back to the time period from January of 1991 until August of 1991. You testified earlier that the armed units in the SAO -- in the SAO Krajina were police units and volunteer units. Can you explain what Milan Martic's role was with respect to these units, these armed units?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Milan Martic set up a camp, a training camp, for special police units and he was in command of that, and there was training for the volunteer units in groups at the same camp, and they too were under the control of the parallel structures of government in Krajina, and Milan Martic was a participant, a member, of all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I want to go through now, please, Milan Martic's formal positions. You already testified about his role in the Council for Popular Resistance or National Resistance in 1990 and also you made reference to his other positions. On the 4th of January 1991, did he receive -- was he appointed to a position?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: He was appointed Secretary of the Interior of the SAO Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How did that come about, that appointment?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: At the meeting of the interim executive council of the SAO Krajina, Mr. David Rastovic suggested we elect a Secretary of the Interior and he went on to propose Milan Martic, and most people agreed, myself included.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Why did you agree?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Well, the majority was in favour, and politically speaking it would have worked against me had I opposed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we see 65 ter Exhibit number 46, please? And if we could --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. Babic, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: I do apologise. Could you switch on the other screen for me because I don't seem to be able to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you see the document in front of you, Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What is it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: It is the minutes from the executive council meeting of the Serb Autonomous Region in Krajina and it was held in 1991 in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we scroll down, please, on the document, to addendum 82? Thank you. And addendum 2, does it read a proposal to appoint Milan Martic from Knin as the Secretary of Interior of Serbian Autonomous Region of Krajina was unanimously upheld?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could the document be admitted into evidence, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number 181, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we have document 65 ter Exhibit number 45, which is actually in evidence as Exhibit 33? I don't think that's the right document. The document I'm looking for is 02172060. I have 2061 up on the screen. I'm looking for 2060, which I believe is Exhibit 33, and 65 ter 45.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I've got 2060 on my screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Oh, you do? Then it's our screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, the important thing is what do you have on your screen? What's the number on the top of the document that you have on your screen?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: 2061. Those are the last digits.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So the witness also has --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You have a problem between the two of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: We'll do this the old-fashioned way, Your Honour. With the assistance of the usher, could this document be shown to the witness, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, do you recognise that document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And just for the record, the number on that document that I've handed to the witness is 02172060 which I believe is Exhibit 33. What is that document, Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: It's a decision about the appointment of the Secretary of the Interior for SAO Krajina signed by me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm not going to move it into evidence because I think it's already in evidence but if it turns out it isn't we'll clear that up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter 44, please, on the computer?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, do you recognise that document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: I do. It's the decision about the setting up of the Secretariat of the Interior of the SAO Krajina dated the 4th of January 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we turn, please, to the -- rather, scroll down to the bottom of this document? Whose name appears there at the bottom?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: My own.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you provide this document to the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Is it an authentic document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: It is, from the archives.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I notice that the document does not have a signature, does not have a stamp on it. Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: It's a document from the archives. As I said, it may happen that the original is submitted and what is filed in the archives is a simple copy without any signatures or stamps, simply registration number, which is a number to the left.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: At the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, could this document be admitted into evidence, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number 182, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we have document number 47, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: I do. This is a telex with information -- a message.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Who is it from?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: This message came from the executive council of the SAO Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And if we could scroll down to the bottom of it, please, whose name appears?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: My own.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What's the date of this document? We will go back to the top of it, please.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: The 5th of January 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Who is it to?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: It is to the president of the SFRY in Belgrade, the federal Secretariat of the Interior in Belgrade, the Minister of the Interior of the Republic of Croatia in Zagreb, the republic Secretariat of the Interior of the Republic of Serbia in Belgrade, the republic Secretariat of the Interior of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Sarajevo, and the police administrations in Zadar, Sibenik, Gospic, Sisak, and to the news agency Tanjug in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now in the first paragraph, it says, it gives a list of the police stations that will be included in the Secretariat. Or rather it gives a list of the municipalities where police stations will be included in the Secretariat, Obrovac, Benkovac, Gracac, and so forth. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, the second paragraph, it says, and I'll read the paragraph, it says, "All human and civil rites shall be guaranteed on the territory of the Autonomous District of Krajina irrespective of the religious, racial and ethnic affiliation of the population." Do you know why -- no, that's -- do you know why that language was included in this document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: It was important at the time to mention all this because of interethnic tensions and an increase in tensions amongst the inhabitants of different nationalities because of various events that had taken place within Krajina itself, conflicts, tensions, information that we received about armed groupings that found themselves in that area and around that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could this document be admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number 183, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we look at 65 ter 646, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, do you see that document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: I do. This refers to an organisation chart of the Secretariat for the Interior and the date is the 19th of January 1991 and the decision was made in Knin. On the part of the executive council of the Serb Autonomous District of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In Article 1, it says that the Secretariat for Internal Affairs carries out all internal affairs in relation to the rights and duties of Serb Autonomous Region of Krajina and that is state security affairs, public security affairs, and other internal affairs. All of those parts were included within the Secretariat for Internal Affairs?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Was this document provided to Mr. Martic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes, and he was behind the draft of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we look at Article 11, please? It's probably on the third page. No, the previous page. Second page, sorry. If you could scroll down, please. I will -- I'm going to read Article 11, please. "The secretary decides on employment and termination of employment in the Secretariat on assignments of the employees, placing them at disposal, giving awards for achieved results, disciplinary responsibility for minor and serious violations of duty, and other issues from the field of working responsibilities in the Secretariat according to this resolution and the enactment from Article 14 of the resolution." How long was this organisational document for the Secretariat of Internal Affairs in place? That is, how long was it in effect, from the 19th of January until when?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Until the 1st of August 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What happened on the 1st of August 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: A decision was reached about the application of the law on internal affairs of the Republic of Serbia on the territory of Krajina. Basically that law started to apply on the territory of the SAO Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That decision of August 11991 is actually included in your written statement, what we refer to as the 89(F) statement, and for the benefit of the court it's tab 41 of the 89(F) statement. Could we have 65 ter Exhibit 1849, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we do that, I've got a question on this document that's on the screen right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Probably be best to proceed with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Right. Can we go to the first page of this document, please? Mr. Babic, Article 2 of this document says, "When by federal law, other law, or regulation from the field of internal affairs, the jurisdiction of bodies for internal affairs, apart from jurisdiction of federal bodies, is determined, those affairs on the territory of Serb Autonomous Region of Krajina are carried out by the Secretariat for Internal Affairs of Serb Autonomous Region of Krajina." What is meant by "federal law" in that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: It's the law of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia and its bodies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour's question reminded me that I need to move this into evidence as well. Could we move this into evidence as well, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is then admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number 184, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, before I go on to the next document, could you tell us, at this time, in January of 1991, was the -- was Martic, Milan Martic, already a part of the parallel structure that you have described?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: He was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, if we could have 65 ter Exhibit 1849, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you recognise this, Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: I do. This is the official journal of the Republic of Serbia from July 1991, where the law on internal affairs was published.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, could this be moved into evidence, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number 185, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Going back a little bit in time, on the 29th of May 1991, was Milan Martic appointed to a position?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was elected by the assembly and he was appointed the Defence Minister of the SAO Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you tell us how this came about?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Following my initiative, I wanted to weaken Mr. Martic by transferring him from the post of the future Minister of the Interior to the post of the Defence Minister. The Defence Minister would have been seen as powerful in terms of the actual title but in terms of the actual remit, it was much less important. And after I made the proposal, I was told by someone that he would accept that with the proviso that he could still maintain his control over the special police units which were being trained at Golubic. And that was when negotiations started and several people participated in those negotiations, one of his aides as well, and he agreed that his name be put forward for the post of the Defence Minister, with the proviso that the special units of the Krajina Militia, being trained within the Ministry of the Interior, be placed under the control of the Defence Ministry and he took his oaths as the Defence Minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Babic, I have some questions about kind of terminology here, and from -- from January of 1991 until the 29th of May of 1991, did Mr. Martic remain in the position as the Secretary of the Interior of the SAO Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you made reference in your previous answer about -- you refer to the future Minister of the Interior. Can you explain to the Court why were these positions being renamed or what was happening at this time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: On the 29th of May 1991, the government of the SAO Krajina was formed. As for the Secretariats, before that time, there was only one for the interior and it was renamed into the Secretariat for Internal Affairs. The name was changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: We may have a translation issue here. It was changed from the Secretariat of the Interior to what? In May of 1991, on the 29th of May 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: The Ministry of the Interior of the SAO Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you've testified that Mr. Martic took his oath as the Defence Minister. How long did he hold that position?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: For a couple of days, not more than that. Formally speaking, he held that position until the 27th of June 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What happened after a couple of days?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: He said he won't do it any more, that he won't be the Minister of Defence, but that he wants to remain as the Minister of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You testified earlier that it was your initiative to put him in the Minister of Defence and that your purpose was to weaken his power. Why did you want to weaken his power?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: As the Secretary of the Interior, he became a powerful man. He was controlling the regular police, the Special Forces of the police that were being formed at Golubic, and at the same time he was neglecting some of the basic tasks and duties of the secretary, that is to protect public order, and because in April and May, there was great turmoil and unrest, in which the police, that is the Ministry of the Interior, participated, and Mr. Martic included.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, you said that after a couple of days, he said he wouldn't be Minister of Defence any more, he wanted to remain as Minister of the Interior. What happened then?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: On those two or three days, the newly appointed Minister of the Interior, Mr. Dusan Vjestica, tried to take over the control of the Minister of the Interior. He issued some appointment orders and he tried to remove some of Martic's aides but Martic and his aides refused with sarcasm, and after a few days everyone accepted that Martic remains where he was, that is he never even left the position. He was previously the Secretary of the Interior. During the next SAO assembly held in Bosanska Grahovo [phoen], during the joint assembly with the Bosnian Krajina assembly, Martic was formally appointed as Minister of the Interior and Dusan Vjestica as Minister of Urban Planning and Public Utility Services.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If Milan Martic made this decision within two or three days, why was he not appointed to the Minister of the Interior until the 27th of June 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: That's when the next assembly session was held.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know why Milan Martic changed his mind about being Minister of Defence?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Frenki and Jovica Stanisic advised him to refuse to be that and that he should remain Minister of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: I was told by some of the people from the police station that the people I mentioned advised him not to accept the new position, and Jovica Stanisic confirmed that to me next year, in 1993, when he said that they made a mistake for not leaving Martic as the Minister of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we see 65 ter number 79, please, which I believe is Exhibit 35.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we do that, is the document on the screen already in evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I believe so, Your Honour, and I'm getting the nod. I think it is in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you recognise that document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. That was the appointment of the minister appointing Milan Martic as Minister of Defence of the SAO Krajina as of the 29th of May 1991, made by the assembly of the Serb Autonomous District of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we see 65 ter Exhibit 75 [sic], please, which I believe is Exhibit 32.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before you move on, let me just be -- now on the 29th of May 1991, the assembly itself appoints Mr. Milan Martic as the Minister of Defence, not Minister of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Your Honour. 65 ter, 78.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. That is the decision to form special-purpose units of the Serbian Autonomous Region of Krajina MUP to be called the Krajina Police, to be under the authority of the Ministry of Defence. The decision is dated the 29th of May 1991, made by the assembly of the SAO.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, during this time that -- during the time from the 29th of May 1991 until the 27th of June 1991, when, formally at least, Mr. Martic was Minister of Defence, did he ever lose control of the police in the SAO Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we look at 65 ter Exhibit 80, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is a decision on the election of the Minister of the Interior of the Serbian Autonomous District of Krajina, Dusan Vjestica, made during the assembly session of the SAO Krajina, held on the 29th of May 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could this be admitted into evidence, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence and may it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number 186, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Finally could we look at 65 ter Exhibit 91, which is Exhibit 34?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is a decision on the election of the Minister of the Interior of the Serbian Autonomous District of Krajina, appointing Milan Martic as Minister of the Interior of the Serbian Autonomous District of Krajina, dated the 27th of June 1991, by the assembly of the SAO Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Until when did Mr. Martic remain in this position?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Until early 1994, when he was elected president of the republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I think this would be a convenient time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What's happening to this document? Is it already an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It is. It's Exhibit 34.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The matter is postponed to tomorrow at quarter past two in the same courtroom. The matter is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe we are in Courtroom I tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Oh, in Courtroom I? Let me just make sure. You are very right. We will be in Courtroom I tomorrow at quarter past two. Thank you very much. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 16th day of February, 2006, at 2.15 p.m. 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
